opus-5.5.text:
I think language plays a very special role, but we have to be careful not to overstate it.

If you look at evolution, intelligence didn't start with language. Animals perceive the world, move through it, grab things, avoid danger, find food. Hundreds of millions of years of evolution went into that sensorimotor intelligence: understanding space, physics, cause and effect through the body. Language showed up very late, maybe tens or a hundred thousand years ago. So in a sense language sits on top of a huge foundation of embodied intelligence that was already there.

What language did was extraordinary, though. It compressed experience into symbols that can be passed between people and across generations. Before language, what one individual learned mostly died with them. After language, and especially after writing, knowledge could accumulate. One person discovers that a certain plant is poisonous, and everyone else learns it without having to eat it. That's why human civilization took off so explosively in a short time. Language turned individual intelligence into collective, cumulative intelligence.

It also changed how we think internally. Abstract concepts like "justice," "number," or "the future" are very hard to hold without language. It gives us a tool for reasoning, planning, and reflecting on ourselves.

This is directly relevant to AI today. Large language models learned from this enormous compressed record of human knowledge, which is why they look so smart so quickly. They inherited the top layer, the abstract, symbolic part. But they skipped the bottom layer. They know the word "cup," and they can describe how to pour water, but they've never actually felt the weight of a cup or seen water spill. A lot of what we know about the physical world was never written down, because to humans it's too obvious to say.

So my view is that language is the key to human-level abstraction and knowledge transfer, but it isn't the whole of intelligence. For machines to have truly general intelligence, especially in the physical world, we have to fill in that embodied foundation, through perception, action, and interaction, and then connect it with the power of language. That combination is what I find most exciting about embodied AI right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes language as enabling abstraction, reasoning, knowledge transfer, and cumulative intelligence, contributing to human civilization’s rapid development.

r002.rationale: It mentions animal intelligence predating language, but does not say that some nonhuman animals have intelligence comparable to young children despite much weaker language abilities.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I think about a lot, because my own work started in computer vision and robotics, and language only entered the picture later. So let me answer it a bit from the outside.

I think language did something very specific for human intelligence: it compressed experience into a form that could be transmitted across individuals and across generations. Before language, every animal had to learn almost everything from its own trial and error. A monkey that figured out how to crack a nut couldn't really hand that knowledge to its grandchildren except by letting them watch. Language changed that. It let one person's hard-won lesson become a sentence that another person could receive in a few seconds. So the first role is accumulation. Human intelligence isn't mainly individual brilliance, it's a stack of knowledge that compounds because it's written down or spoken.

The second role, which I think is less discussed, is that language gave us a handle on abstraction. When you name something, you can manipulate it without having it in front of you. You can talk about "tomorrow" or "fairness" or "a thousand." These aren't things you can point at. Language gave the brain symbols to operate on, and once you have symbols you can do planning, counterfactuals, mathematics. A lot of what we call reasoning is really the manipulation of linguistic symbols in a controlled way.

But I want to be careful here, because I think there's a tendency, especially now with large language models, to overestimate language. Language is a very lossy compression of the world. When I say "pick up the cup," the words carry almost none of the information actually needed to pick up the cup. The friction, the weight, the position of your fingers, the fact that it's half full and will slosh. All of that lives in your body and your perception, not in the sentence. Children learn most of their physical understanding of the world before they can speak fluently. So language sits on top of a huge non-verbal foundation, and it's that foundation that makes the words mean anything.

So my view is that language was the key that unlocked collective, cumulative intelligence, and the tool that enabled abstract thought. But it's not where intelligence comes from. It's more like the interface between intelligences. That's actually why I find embodied AI so interesting right now. We've built systems that are extraordinarily good at the interface layer, and the open question is whether you can get real understanding of the world by going through the interface alone, or whether, like a child, you have to touch things first.

r001.rationale: The response describes language as unlocking collective, cumulative intelligence and enabling abstract thought, identifying it as a major step in human intelligence.

r002.rationale: It mentions monkeys and children, but does not claim that some nonhuman animals have intelligence comparable to young children despite weaker language abilities.

astra-6.text:
I think language plays two roles. It’s a way to communicate, but it’s also a tool for organizing thought. Once we can name something, we can refer to it when it isn’t in front of us, compare it with other things, and build more abstract ideas around it. We can talk about what happened yesterday, what might happen tomorrow, or what would happen under different conditions.

And language lets intelligence accumulate across people and generations. You discover something, explain it to me, and I don’t have to repeat your entire process of discovery. I can start from what you’ve learned. That makes knowledge a collective achievement.

But I wouldn’t equate language with intelligence. We also think through perception, movement, and spatial relationships, sometimes without words. So I see language as an amplifier: it helps us organize and share those abilities, and that sharing changes how much we can learn and accomplish together.

r001.rationale: The response describes language as a tool for organizing thought and accumulating shared knowledge, and calls it an amplifier that changes what people can learn and accomplish together.

r002.rationale: The response mentions nonverbal thinking in general but does not say that some nonhuman animals show intelligence comparable to young children despite weaker language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language plays two roles: it helps us organize our own thinking, and it allows us to share thinking with other people. When we put an idea into words, we can examine it, question it, and connect it to other ideas. That gives us a powerful way to reason beyond what is immediately in front of us.

But the social role may be even more important. Language lets one person learn from another person’s experience without having to repeat it. Knowledge can accumulate across generations, and people can coordinate around increasingly complex goals. In that sense, human intelligence develops not just inside individual brains, but through communication between them.

I wouldn’t say all intelligence depends on language. We also think through perception, movement, and images. I see language as something that amplifies those capacities—and then changes what we can do with them.

r001.rationale: The response says language amplifies reasoning and enables knowledge to accumulate across generations and coordination on complex goals, presenting it as a major contributor to developing human intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention nonhuman animals, comparisons with young children, or their weaker language abilities.
